industry.ipm: The Indian pharmaceutical market (IPM) grew 10.0% in the twelve months to Jun-2026 and 12.2% in the Apr-Jun 2026 quarter (IQVIA, as quoted by Glenmark). Growth is roughly half volume, a quarter new products and a quarter price; prices of drugs on the price-control list (NLEM) can rise only by the wholesale-price index each April. Distribution changed in FY26: the GST rate cut announced in Aug-2025 made distributors run down stock, which hit companies with a three-tier (super-stockist) system like Glenmark far harder than peers using carrying-and-forwarding agents.
industry.usGenerics: US generics are a price-erosion business (low-to-mid single digits a year on the base) where profit comes from products few rivals can make: inhalers (MDIs, DPIs), nasal sprays, complex injectables, and first-to-file or CGT exclusivities worth 180 days or more. Approvals depend on plant inspections: an Official Action Indicated (OAI) rating or a warning letter blocks new approvals from that site.
industry.europe: Europe is a mix of tendered generics and branded products. Glenmark is shifting to brands (respiratory: Ryaltris and MDIs; dermatology: Winlevi, Hilkota), ~30% of its European sales today with a target of ~60% in five years (CMD, Q1FY27 call).
industry.emergingMarkets: Emerging markets (Russia/CIS, Latin America, Middle East & Africa, Asia-Pacific) are branded-generic markets where Glenmark ranks 8th in Russian dermatology (IQVIA) and Ryaltris is the leading allergy nasal spray in most launched markets. They carry currency risk (rouble, Latin American currencies) and are the main outlet for in-licensed oncology drugs (Aumolertinib, Trastuzumab Rezetecan, envafolimab) and, eventually, ISB 2001 outside AbbVie's territories.
industry.innovation: Indian companies rarely monetise new drugs; Glenmark's earlier out-licensing deals (oglemilast, melogliptin, 2004-2008) failed in the clinic. ISB 2001 (Jul-2025, US$700mn upfront), which the company calls a landmark deal, changed that; its value from here depends on AbbVie's development decisions, which Glenmark does not control.

moat.evidence: No.2 in dermatology, No.3 respiratory, No.4 cardiac (IQVIA MAT Jun-26); 11 brands in the IPM top 300 (Telma, Ascoril, Candid, Alex); secondary sales 1.5x the market over three years
moat.soWhat: The most valuable and durable part of Glenmark; but a 2.37% share (No.13) and a channel model that broke twice (Q3FY24, Q2FY26)

moat.evidence: Ryaltris: own combination nasal spray in 57 markets, >US$100mn sales, +40-50% secondary growth; first generic Flovent 44 with CGT exclusivity; world's first nebulised triple therapy in India
moat.soWhat: Real capability that few Indian peers have; US respiratory generics are still small for Glenmark

moat.evidence: ISB 2001 licensed to AbbVie for US$700mn upfront; ISB 2301 IND by end-2026; ~US$70mn a year burn; earlier deals (2004-2008) failed
moat.soWhat: Proven once; future value depends on clinical outcomes and partners, not on Glenmark's commercial strength

moat.evidence: NA core sales flat at ~Rs3,000-3,150 cr for five years; three USFDA warning letters since 2022 (Goa, Monroe, Indore); 'mostly commodity injectables' (CMD)
moat.soWhat: A price-taking business; compliance has cost launches before

moat.evidence: Europe the fastest-growing region for four years (CMD) but only high single digit in FY27; Russia dermatology No.8; in-licensed oncology for EM
moat.soWhat: Good distribution reach; brands are mostly in-licensed or partnered, so margins are shared

moat.evidence: Core EBITDA margin 16.6% in Q1FY27 vs 25-30% for Sun, Cipla, Torrent; net cash only after the one-off upfront; working capital ~107-115 days
moat.soWhat: Glenmark earns less on each rupee of sales than its large peers
